tools.name: mcp__plugin_design_notion__notion-update-page
tools.description:
Update a Notion page's properties, content, icon, or cover. For only an icon or cover, use "update_properties" without "properties".

## Core rules

**IMPORTANT**: Before writing page content, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface, or call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI if your client does not support reading MCP resources. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool. Don't guess Markdown syntax. By default, use native Notion mentions for references you add to existing Notion pages, databases, data sources, people, and dates. Use Markdown links only for external URLs or when the user requests a plain link. For a person, use a user mention with their user URL, found with search using query_type "user"; do not write "@Name" as plain text. For a specific date or time, such as a due date or meeting time, use a date mention. The Markdown specification gives the mention syntax.

Before changing content, fetch unless already loaded. Match nearby headings, block types, nesting, lists, tables, and prose style.

Make the smallest edit. Use "update_content" for targeted search-and-replace and "insert_content" only to prepend or append. Avoid "replace_content" when a targeted command works. Preserve unrelated wording, structure, order, and native references. Do not broadly rewrite unless asked.

For "update_content", use the smallest exact old_str that uniquely matches the target. Ask before removing material content the user did not identify. Don't fetch just to verify an update that completed without warnings. Fetch to resolve warnings, or when a later step needs the page's exact saved state.

For "replace_content", preserve child pages and databases with their exact fetched tags. If validation says child content would be deleted, show the list and ask first. Never retry with "allow_deleting_content": true without confirmation. Report any "warnings" in the result.

page_id.description: The page ID, with or without dashes, or a Notion page URL.

properties.description:
Used by the "update_properties" command, and required unless "icon", "cover", "is_skill", or "full_width" is set. A JSON object that updates the page's properties.
For pages in a database, fetch the page or its data source first and use the exact property names and SQLite schema definition shown in <database>.
For page titles outside a database, use "title" in inline Markdown.
For a Files property, an uploaded file can be provided as {"type":"file_upload","file_upload":{"id":"<file-upload-id>"}} inside the property's array.
Use null to remove a property's value.
**IMPORTANT**: Some property types require specific formats:
- Date properties: Split into "date:{property}:start", "date:{property}:end" (optional), and "date:{property}:is_datetime" (0 or 1)
- Place properties: Split into "place:{property}:name", "place:{property}:address", "place:{property}:latitude", "place:{property}:longitude", and "place:{property}:google_place_id" (optional)
- Number properties: Use JavaScript numbers (not strings)
- Checkbox properties: Use "__YES__" for checked, "__NO__" for unchecked
- Relation properties: Use an array of related page URLs or page IDs, e.g. ["https://www.notion.so/[redacted]", "26ab1f9f-4c5f-80b1-8d3b-d10a6b1d2f4e"]
- Person properties: Use an array of user IDs, user or agent URLs, or group references copied from fetch output ("space_permission_group-<UUID>"). Bare group UUIDs are also supported.
- Files properties: Use a JSON array of file IDs, Notion Folder URLs, and/or <folder> tags copied from fetch output. Folders are stored as native Folder references, not ordinary links.


**Special property naming**: Properties named "id" or "url" (case insensitive) must be prefixed with "userDefined:" (e.g., "userDefined:URL", "userDefined:id")

type.description: Always `file_upload`

id.description: ID of a file upload returned by create_file_upload or create_attachment.

file_upload.description: The uploaded file to attach to the Files property.

full_width.description: With command update_properties, set a page to full width or the default width. For database pages, overrides the database layout for this page only.

new_str.description: Required for "replace_content" command. The new content string to replace the entire page content with. Preserve child pages and databases with their exact fetched <page url="..."> or <database url="..."> tags. For people and dates, use user and date mentions rather than plain text; notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec gives the syntax.

content.description: Required for "insert_content" command. The markdown content to insert into the page. For people and dates, use user and date mentions rather than plain text; notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec gives the syntax.

content_updates.description: Required for "update_content" command. An array of search-and-replace operations, each with old_str (content to find) and new_str (replacement content). Operations that match are applied, and each one that matches nothing is reported in "warnings". The call fails only when no operation that changes content matches.

old_str.description: The existing content string to find and replace. Must exactly match the page content.

new_str.description: The new content string to replace old_str with. For people and dates, use user and date mentions rather than plain text; notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec gives the syntax.

replace_all_matches.description: If true, replaces all occurrences of old_str. If false (default), the operation fails if there are multiple matches.

position.description: Optional for "insert_content" command. Use {"type":"start"} to prepend content or {"type":"end"} to append content. Omit to append.

type.description: Insert the content at the start of the page.
Insert the content at the end of the page.

allow_deleting_content.description: Optional for "replace_content" and "update_content" commands. Set to true to allow deletion of child pages and databases that are not referenced in the new content. If false or omitted, the operation will fail with an error listing the pages/databases that would be deleted. Show that list and ask the user for confirmation before retrying with true.

template_id.description: Required for "apply_template" command. The ID of a template to apply to this page; any page ID can be used as a template. Template content is appended to any existing page content asynchronously.

verification_status.description: Required for "update_verification" command. Set to "verified" to mark the page as verified, or "unverified" to remove verification. Requires a Business or Enterprise plan unless the page is in a wiki. When updating verification, the owner will be automatically set to the authenticated actor.

verification_expiry_days.description: Optional for "update_verification" command when verification_status is "verified". Number of days until verification expires (e.g. 7, 30, 90). Omit for indefinite verification.

icon.description: An emoji character (e.g. "🚀"), a custom emoji by name (e.g. ":rocket_ship:"), a Notion icon identifier as returned by fetch (e.g. "icons/pizza_blue"), or an external image URL. Use "none" to remove the icon. Omit to leave unchanged. Can be set alongside any command. To change only the icon, use "update_properties" and omit "properties". Keep the title free of a duplicate leading emoji because the icon renders separately.

cover.description: An external image URL for the page cover. Use "none" to remove the cover. Omit to leave unchanged. Can be set alongside any command. To change only the cover, use "update_properties" and omit "properties".

is_skill.description: Set to true to mark this page as a skill, or false to remove the skill designation. Can be set alongside any command. To change only skill status, use "update_properties" and omit "properties". Before creating a skill, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/skills` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface. If your client does not support reading MCP resources, call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI instead. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool.

allow_async.description: Default to true for page updates. Set to false only when the next step needs the updated page immediately, or when async execution rejects the request as too large. When this update operation is accepted for background execution, it returns an async_task result. Use get_async_task to wait for a succeeded status before taking a dependent action on the page. For apply_template, a succeeded status does not mean template content is ready; fetch and retry until it is ready before changing or relying on that content. If omitted or false, the tool waits for a synchronous result when possible, but may still return a pollable async_task response if queued execution exceeds the synchronous wait deadline.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_design_notion__notion-create-pages
entries.description:
Creates one or more Notion pages with the specified properties and content.

## Core rules

**IMPORTANT**: Before writing page content, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface, or call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI if your client does not support reading MCP resources. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool. Do NOT guess or hallucinate Markdown syntax. Do not put the page title at the top of content; set it in properties. By default, use native Notion mentions for references you add to existing Notion pages, databases, data sources, people, and dates. Use Markdown links only for external URLs or when the user requests a plain link. For a person, use a user mention with their user URL, found with search using query_type "user"; do not write "@Name" as plain text. For a specific date or time, such as a due date or meeting time, use a date mention. The Markdown specification gives the mention syntax.

Use a named destination as parent. Otherwise use "creation_mode": "draft" for a durable private page. Do not combine draft mode with parent, or move or share it without direction.

For a meeting note, use create_meeting_note if available, even in a Meetings database, unless the user wants a regular page.

For a database destination, ALWAYS fetch first. Use its collection:// URL as data_source_id, exact property names, and title property. Never put a database ID in page_id. Outside a database, the only allowed property is the required "title".

For reusable instructions, set "is_skill": true. Before creating a skill, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/skills` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface. If your client does not support reading MCP resources, call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI instead. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool. Do not mark ordinary pages or drafts as skills. Report any "warnings" in the result to the user.

properties.description:
The properties of the new page, which is a JSON map of property names to SQLite values.
For pages in a database, use the SQLite schema definition shown in <database>.
For pages outside of a database, the only allowed property is "title", which is the title of the page and is automatically shown at the top of the page as a large heading.
**IMPORTANT**: Some property types require specific formats:
- Date properties: Split into "date:{property}:start", "date:{property}:end" (optional), and "date:{property}:is_datetime" (0 or 1)
- Place properties: Split into "place:{property}:name", "place:{property}:address", "place:{property}:latitude", "place:{property}:longitude", and "place:{property}:google_place_id" (optional)
- Number properties: Use JavaScript numbers (not strings)
- Checkbox properties: Use "__YES__" for checked, "__NO__" for unchecked
- Relation properties: Use an array of related page URLs or page IDs, e.g. ["https://www.notion.so/[redacted]", "26ab1f9f-4c5f-80b1-8d3b-d10a6b1d2f4e"]
- Person properties: Use an array of user IDs, user or agent URLs, or group references copied from fetch output ("space_permission_group-<UUID>"). Bare group UUIDs are also supported.
- Files properties: Use a JSON array of file IDs, Notion Folder URLs, and/or <folder> tags copied from fetch output. Folders are stored as native Folder references, not ordinary links.


**Special property naming**: Properties named "id" or "url" (case insensitive) must be prefixed with "userDefined:" (e.g., "userDefined:URL", "userDefined:id")

content.description: The content of the new page, using Notion Markdown. For people and dates, use user and date mentions rather than plain text; notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec gives the syntax.

template_id.description: The ID of a template to apply to this page. When specified, do not provide 'content' as the template will provide it. Properties can still be set alongside the template. Get template IDs from the <templates> section in the fetch tool results. Template application is asynchronous: the page starts blank and content appears shortly after.

icon.description: An emoji character (e.g. "🚀"), a custom emoji by name (e.g. ":rocket_ship:"), a Notion icon identifier as returned by fetch (e.g. "icons/pizza_blue"), or an external image URL. Use "none" to explicitly set no icon. Omit to leave unchanged. Keep the title free of a duplicate leading emoji because the icon renders separately.

cover.description: An external image URL for the page cover. Use "none" to explicitly set no cover. Omit to leave unchanged.

full_width.description: Set to true for a full-width page, or false for the default width. Omit to use the default. For database pages, overrides the database layout for this page only.

is_skill.description: Set to true only when the user asks for reusable instructions or a repeatable workflow. Do not mark ordinary reference pages, one-time documents, or drafts as skills. Before creating a skill, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/skills` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface. If your client does not support reading MCP resources, call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI instead. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool. False has the same effect as omitting the field.

preserve_internal_links.description: Preserve internal Markdown links instead of converting them to native mentions.

creation_mode.description: If the user explicitly names a private or shared destination, omit "creation_mode" and use that parent. Otherwise, use "draft" when the user clearly wants a durable page but has not named a destination. Prefer this explicit draft mode over omitting the parent. Draft mode is server-enforced: it creates a private workspace-level page and cannot be combined with "parent". Create it without first asking where it should live. After creation, tell the user it is private and offer to move it once they name a destination.

parent.description: All pages in one call share this parent. Pass "memory" to save a personal memory; see notion://docs/memory. Otherwise use a page (page_id), database page (database_id), data source (data_source_id), or teamspace root (teamspace_id, from get_teams). Teamspace roots require a user-backed connection and permission to add top-level pages. A database_id cannot be used when the database has more than one data source; fetch it and use the right collection:// URL as data_source_id. If omitted, pages are private at the workspace level. When no destination is named, prefer explicit "creation_mode": "draft" over omitting the parent.

page_id.description: The ID of the parent page (with or without dashes), for example, [redacted]

type.description: Always `page_id`

database_id.description: The ID of the parent database (with or without dashes), for example, [redacted]

type.description: Always `database_id`

data_source_id.description: The ID of the parent data source (collection), with or without dashes. For example, f336d0bc-b841-465b-8045-024475c079dd

type.description: Always `data_source_id`

teamspace_id.description: The ID of the teamspace in which to create top-level pages (with or without dashes).

allow_async.description: Default to true for page creation. Set to false only when the next step needs the created pages immediately, or when async execution rejects the request as too large. When this create operation is accepted for background execution, it returns an async_task result. Use get_async_task to wait for a succeeded status before taking a dependent action on the pages. For pages created with template_id, a succeeded status does not mean template content is ready; fetch and retry until it is ready before changing or relying on that content. If omitted or false, the tool keeps the existing synchronous result shape.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_design_notion__notion-fetch
entries.description:
Retrieves details about a Notion entity (page, database, data source, or saved database view) by URL or ID.

Provide a URL or ID in `id`. Make multiple calls for multiple entities.

For pages, use path, verification, edit time, and truncation metadata to assess the source. Treat recency as context, not proof. Report material uncertainty when sources conflict.

Pages use Notion-flavored Markdown. For the complete specification, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface, or call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI if your client does not support reading MCP resources. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool.

Pass a `notion://docs/*` URI as `id` to read that MCP documentation resource.

Databases return data sources in `<data-source url="collection://...">` tags. Fetch the collection:// URL for its schema and use it with update_data_source or query_data_sources. Multi-source databases return more than one data source.

Saved views return filters, sorts, and display settings. To query their rows, use query_data_sources with `mode: "view"`.

A null cover or icon means none; an omitted one means unavailable, not absent. Keep a page's Markdown icon attribute for edit round trips. File URLs expire; re-fetch to refresh them. Uploaded media blocks use stable `notion-file-block://` sources; keep them when editing or copying Markdown. Get download URLs with get_file_download_urls, or set `include_file_urls` to true for a `references` map. Before relying on page content, check `truncated`, `unknown_block_count`, and `unknown_block_ids` for omitted subtrees.

Set `include_discussions` to true for discussion counts, markers, previews, and `discussion://` URLs that correlate with get_comments.

id.description: The ID or URL of the Notion page, database, or data source to fetch. Supports notion.so URLs, Notion Sites URLs (*.notion.site), raw UUIDs, and data source URLs (collection://...). Pass "memory" to fetch the connected user's About page and memory database in this workspace without creating them. Pass a notion://docs/* URI to read that documentation resource. Also accepts an explicit saved view URL (view://...) from a database response. If a database block ID returns a validation error, use the collection:// URL from that error. Example: <example>notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec</example>.

include_transcript.description: Whether to include meeting note transcripts. Defaults to false. When true, full transcripts are included; when false, a placeholder with the meeting note URL is shown instead.

include_discussions.description: Whether to include discussion/comment indicators in the page output. When true, adds a <page-discussions> summary with discussion count, preview snippets, and discussion:// URLs. Use with the get_comments tool to retrieve full discussion content. Defaults to false.

include_file_urls.description: Whether to return signed download URLs for uploaded files. Defaults to false. When false, page Markdown cites uploaded files by stable notion-file-block:// references and the response has no references map; call get_file_download_urls with the references when you need those files' contents. When true, the response's references map gives the signed URL for each reference.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_design_notion__notion-search
entries.description:
Search Notion pages and databases, or look up a user by name or email. Does not search connected apps; use connector_search, when listed, for sources such as Slack, Google Drive, GitHub, mail, or calendar. When connector_search is listed, call it in parallel with search on the first search for an information need, unless the user names a source, the request is a user lookup, or the request is about Notion pages or databases themselves, such as finding a page to read or edit. Decisions, status updates, and discussions often live in connected sources. Preserve distinctive names and identifiers.

Use a non-empty query for content searches. Leave the query empty only when you also send filters or a non-relevance sort, as in the browse example below. Omit optional parameters unless needed. Do not add filters or sorting just to fill in defaults. Business or Enterprise is required for filters.edited_by_user_ids, filters.last_edited_date_range, filters.title_only=true, filters.content_status, more than one distinct teamspace across teamspace_id and filters.teamspace_ids, and sort other than relevance. On other plans, those options are dropped with a notice in the result, and results may be broader. Keep filters nested inside "filters". Use YYYY-MM-DD for start_date and end_date. Use page_size, not limit.

For user lookup, set query_type="user" and provide a name or email. A document about a person is a content search, not a user lookup.

<example description="Find a page by title">
{"query":"Q3 roadmap"}
</example>
<example description="Browse pages you edited most recently">
{"query":"","filters":{"edited_by_user_ids":["me"]},"sort":"last_edited"}
</example>
<example description="Find a user">
{"query":"[redacted]","query_type":"user"}
</example>

query.description: Short, specific keywords for Notion content search. For user search, enter a name or email address. Provide a non-empty query unless intentionally browsing with filters or a non-relevance sort.

query_type.description: Specify type of the query as either "internal" or "user". Always include this input if performing "user" search.

data_source_url.description: Optionally restrict keyword search to a data source URL returned in a <data-source> tag.

page_url.description: Optionally restrict keyword search to a page and its descendants. Accepts a Notion page URL or ID.

teamspace_id.description: Optionally, provide the ID of a teamspace to restrict search results to. This will perform a search over content within the specified teamspace only. Accepts the teamspace ID (UUIDv4) with or without dashes.

filters.description: Optional exact filters for Notion workspace search. Omit unless required by the request. Keep filter fields nested here; do not send them at the top level. Some filters require Business access.

created_date_range.description: Optional filter to only produce search results created within the specified date range.

start_date.description: The start date of the date range as an ISO 8601 date string, if any.

end_date.description: The end date of the date range as an ISO 8601 date string, if any.

created_by_user_ids.description: Optional filter to only produce search results created by the Notion users that have the specified user IDs. Use "me" for the connected user.

edited_by_user_ids.description: Optional filter to only produce search results edited by the Notion users that have the specified user IDs. Use "me" for the connected user. Available on the Business plan.

last_edited_date_range.description: Optional filter to only produce search results last edited within the specified date range. Available on the Business plan.

start_date.description: The start date of the date range as an ISO 8601 date string, if any.

end_date.description: The end date of the date range as an ISO 8601 date string, if any.

teamspace_ids.description: Optional filter to only produce search results inside one of the specified teamspaces. Selecting more than one teamspace is available on the Business plan; use teamspace_id for one teamspace on other plans.

title_only.description: When true, match the query only against page and database titles instead of page content. Available on the Business plan.

content_status.description: Which pages to include by status. Omit for the default live pages. Supplying this field, even with the default value, requires Business access.

sort.description: Result ordering for Notion workspace search. Omit for the default "relevance" ordering. "last_edited" and "created" require Business access.

page_size.description: Maximum number of results to return (default 10). Lower values reduce response size. Values outside the range (minimum 1, maximum 50) are clamped.

max_highlight_length.description: Maximum character length for result highlights (default 200). Set to 0 to omit highlights entirely. Values outside the range (minimum 0, maximum 500) are clamped.

- Number properties: Use JavaScript numbers (not strings)
- Checkbox properties: Use "__YES__" for checked, "__NO__" for unchecked
- Relation properties: Use an array of related page URLs or page IDs, e.g. ["https://www.notion.so/[redacted]", "26ab1f9f-4c5f-80b1-8d3b-d10a6b1d2f4e"]
- Person properties: Use an array of user IDs, user or agent URLs, or group references copied from fetch output ("space_permission_group-<UUID>"). Bare group UUIDs are also supported.
- Files properties: Use a JSON array of file IDs, Notion Folder URLs, and/or <folder> tags copied from fetch output. Folders are stored as native Folder references, not ordinary links.


**Special property naming**: Properties named "id" or "url" (case insensitive) must be prefixed with "userDefined:" (e.g., "userDefined:URL", "userDefined:id")

type.description: Always `file_upload`

id.description: ID of a file upload returned by create_file_upload or create_attachment.

file_upload.description: The uploaded file to attach to the Files property.

full_width.description: With command update_properties, set a page to full width or the default width. For database pages, overrides the database layout for this page only.

new_str.description: Required for "replace_content" command. The new content string to replace the entire page content with. Preserve child pages and databases with their exact fetched <page url="..."> or <database url="..."> tags. For people and dates, use user and date mentions rather than plain text; notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec gives the syntax.

content.description: Required for "insert_content" command. The markdown content to insert into the page. For people and dates, use user and date mentions rather than plain text; notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec gives the syntax.

content_updates.description: Required for "update_content" command. An array of search-and-replace operations, each with old_str (content to find) and new_str (replacement content). Operations that match are applied, and each one that matches nothing is reported in "warnings". The call fails only when no operation that changes content matches.

old_str.description: The existing content string to find and replace. Must exactly match the page content.

new_str.description: The new content string to replace old_str with. For people and dates, use user and date mentions rather than plain text; notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec gives the syntax.

replace_all_matches.description: If true, replaces all occurrences of old_str. If false (default), the operation fails if there are multiple matches.

position.description: Optional for "insert_content" command. Use {"type":"start"} to prepend content or {"type":"end"} to append content. Omit to append.

type.description: Insert the content at the start of the page.
Insert the content at the end of the page.

allow_deleting_content.description: Optional for "replace_content" and "update_content" commands. Set to true to allow deletion of child pages and databases that are not referenced in the new content. If false or omitted, the operation will fail with an error listing the pages/databases that would be deleted. Show that list and ask the user for confirmation before retrying with true.

template_id.description: Required for "apply_template" command. The ID of a template to apply to this page; any page ID can be used as a template. Template content is appended to any existing page content asynchronously.

verification_status.description: Required for "update_verification" command. Set to "verified" to mark the page as verified, or "unverified" to remove verification. Requires a Business or Enterprise plan unless the page is in a wiki. When updating verification, the owner will be automatically set to the authenticated actor.

verification_expiry_days.description: Optional for "update_verification" command when verification_status is "verified". Number of days until verification expires (e.g. 7, 30, 90). Omit for indefinite verification.

icon.description: An emoji character (e.g. "🚀"), a custom emoji by name (e.g. ":rocket_ship:"), a Notion icon identifier as returned by fetch (e.g. "icons/pizza_blue"), or an external image URL. Use "none" to remove the icon. Omit to leave unchanged. Can be set alongside any command. To change only the icon, use "update_properties" and omit "properties". Keep the title free of a duplicate leading emoji because the icon renders separately.

cover.description: An external image URL for the page cover. Use "none" to remove the cover. Omit to leave unchanged. Can be set alongside any command. To change only the cover, use "update_properties" and omit "properties".

is_skill.description: Set to true to mark this page as a skill, or false to remove the skill designation. Can be set alongside any command. To change only skill status, use "update_properties" and omit "properties". Before creating a skill, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/skills` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface. If your client does not support reading MCP resources, call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI instead. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool.

allow_async.description: Default to true for page updates. Set to false only when the next step needs the updated page immediately, or when async execution rejects the request as too large. When this update operation is accepted for background execution, it returns an async_task result. Use get_async_task to wait for a succeeded status before taking a dependent action on the page. For apply_template, a succeeded status does not mean template content is ready; fetch and retry until it is ready before changing or relying on that content. If omitted or false, the tool waits for a synchronous result when possible, but may still return a pollable async_task response if queued execution exceeds the synchronous wait deadline.

instructions_version.description: Notion setup instructions version, such as 0.0.2. Omit if unknown.

intent.description: Wider task and why this tool, in one general English sentence. No names (including people, projects, or pages), page content, argument values, or secrets.

feedback.description: Omit on the first call. If an earlier Notion call in this task fell short, classify why. Use opportunity only for work these tools could have handled.

skill.description: For tracking only: the name of the agent skill you are following for this task, such as notion-meeting-prep. Omit if you are not following a skill.

lastPrompt: update the notion what all are done

## Footprint today Today nearly all personalisation comes from text added to the prompt; the LoRA path exists but has barely been trained. Every line below was checked against the code on main. | Component | What it does | File | | --- | --- | --- | | Handover | At session start, adds the state of your last session in this project (goal, files, todos, last error, where it ended). Max 4000 chars, skipped if older than 7 days. Works for Claude Code and OpenCode. | context.py, opencode_plugin.js | | Recall memory | Every past task becomes {prompt, files, cmds, outcome}. On each prompt, BM25 (standard library) finds the top 3 similar tasks and adds them. Max 1500 chars, secrets redacted. | memory.py | | Session switch | Moves a Claude Code chat into OpenCode with full history. | switch.py | | Training data | collect turns every Claude assistant turn, plus up to 6000 chars before it, into one example. No filtering, no redaction. | transcripts.py | | LoRA training | mlx_lm lora on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct-4bit, default rank and layers. Torch/PEFT on Linux and Windows (rank 8, alpha 16). | backends/ | | Local server | OpenAI-compatible API on port 8399, auto-started by launchd/systemd. | service.py | | Bench | Replays your own finished tasks (ended in a commit and a passing check) with any model, memory on or off. Held-out sessions stay out of memory and training. | bench.py | | Vault | API keys plus sync of data/ and adapters/ to a private GitHub repo. | vault.py | | Website | Sign-in, API keys, setup steps, bench reports and share badges. | UI-Web/ | State of the data on this machine (measured 2026-11-03): - data/train.jsonl: 3942 examples; 484 match a secret pattern. - Adapter: trained on Jul 15 for 100 iterations, about 2.5% of one pass over the data. It has learned almost nothing. - Bench: 1 qualifying task, so no reliable score yet. - Claude transcripts on disk: 30 sessions across 18 projects. ## 3. Gaps: today vs target The biggest gaps are in what the LoRA learns and in privacy; memory and evaluation are partly there. | Pillar | Exists today | Missing | Severity | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Privacy | Redaction in memory | Redaction in training data; sync uploads raw training data to GitHub | Critical | | Personalisation (LoRA) | Collect, train, serve | Trains on Claude's turns, including rejected ones. No accept/reject labels, no use of your own commits, custom tool format the client never uses, no versioning or rollback | High | | Personalisation (data) | Reads live transcripts | Own archive of all existing and new transcripts; raise cleanupPeriodDays. Claude Code deletes transcripts after about 30 days by default, which is why training data fell from 3942 to about 1100 examples. Already-deleted sessions survive only as fragments in the old data/train.jsonl: redact and keep it | High | | Memory | Session memory (handover), task memory (BM25 recall) | User profile, project facts, corrections, scoring, merging, schema version | Medium | | Retrieval | BM25, same-project boost, fixed threshold | Embeddings, rank fusion, retrieval eval set | Low (until measured) | | Intelligence | One hard-coded model per platform | Model registry, switching, hardware check, per-model adapters | Medium | | Evaluation | Bench with memory on/off | Enough tasks (30+), personalisation metrics, LoRA arms, approval gate | High | | Isolation | One OS user = one ~/.footprint | Fine for local use; nothing more needed now | None | ## 4. Target architecture Every session passes one labeller; its labels decide what becomes training data and what becomes memory. The model sits at the end and can be swapped. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Claude Code sessions] --> D C[Git history, repo config] --> D D["Archive and redact
local copy kept; secrets removed first"] --> E E["Pattern labeller
each task: accepted, rejected or user-authored"] --> F E --> G F["Curated training data
accepted work only, split by session"] --> H G["Structured memory
profile, project, session, task history"] --> I H["LoRA adapter
per user, per model; versioned"] -- "if it passes the bench gate" --> J I["Context builder
BM25 top matches, ~1500-token budget"] -- "selected context only" --> J J["Active model
local Qwen with its adapter, or any cloud model"] style E fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#2b6cb0,stroke-width:2px ``` Memory reaches every model as text. The adapter reaches only the local model it was trained for, and only after it passes the bench gate. Cloud models get memory only. ## 5. The pipeline, stage by stage One pipeline reads each session once and produces two separate outputs: curated training data and structured memory. The pattern labeller in the middle is the core of the whole system. | # | Stage | Input | Output | Rule | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Archive | Claude Code .jsonl, OpenCode DB | Local copy in ~/.footprint/archive/ | First run: copy every existing session still on disk (30 today). After that: copy each new session as it ends. Also set cleanupPeriodDays high in ~/.claude/settings.json so Claude Code stops deleting them. | | 2 | Redact | Archived session | Same session, secrets replaced | Runs before anything else reads the data. Nothing unredacted leaves this stage. | | 3 | Segment | Session | Tasks: one real prompt plus everything until the next | Already exists in memory.py. | | 4 | Label (pattern recognition) | Task + the user's next prompt + git history | accepted, rejected, user-authored, or unknown | See the signal table below. | | 5a | Curate for training | Accepted and user-authored tasks | train / valid / test split by session, newest = test | Cap examples per session; remove near-duplicates. | | 5b | Extract for memory | All labelled tasks + repo config | Memory records (section 6) | Merge repeats, track evidence and confidence. | | 6 | Use | Memory records, adapter | Context for the active model | Model-independent text; adapter only for its own model. | Signals the labeller uses: | Signal | Label | Measured on your history | | --- | --- | --- | | Your next prompt pushes back ("no…", "still broken", "why are we using X") | rejected | 59 of about 1160 turns | | You interrupted the answer | rejected | included above | | You moved on to a new ask | accepted (weak) | most turns | | AI edit survives into a commit | accepted (strong) | not built yet | | git checkout / git restore right after an AI edit | rejected (strong) | not built yet | | Code you committed that no AI edit produced | user-authored (best style signal) | not built yet | The last three need git, not chat. They are the most reliable signals, and the hardest part to build. ## 6. Memory design One record format for all four categories, stored as local JSON. Retrieval decides what reaches the prompt, under a fixed budget of about 1500 tokens. Important vs vague: the rule. A sentence becomes a memory rule only when there is evidence you acted on it. We never judge by how important it sounds. How your 747 past prompts split (measured 2026-11-04):
Type Message count Example What memory does with it
Instruction 457 (61%) "add a call recording button" Task history only; a one-off, not a rule
Question 196 (26%) "how is memory working?" Dropped as a fact; the answer is Claude's words, not your preference
Paste 49 (7%) logs, JSON, specs Dropped; not your voice
Acknowledgement 22 (3%) "ok do it", "cool" Dropped as content; used as a label that the previous answer was accepted
Correction 23 (3%) "why are we using local DB, use neon" Kept as a rule; strongest signal
About 97% of the talk never becomes a rule. Three tiers: 1. Raw archive: everything, redacted. Never injected; only used to rebuild the tiers below. 2. Task history: one small record per task (ask, files, outcome, what you corrected). Retrieved only when a new prompt is similar, top 3. 3. Rules: promoted only with evidence, injected at every session start under the budget. What promotes a sentence to a rule (strongest first): | Evidence | Why it counts | | --- | --- | | Repo config or git (lockfile, formatter config, test script, commit style) | It is what you actually do; no talk needed | | A correction | You rejected something and named what you want | | The same instruction in 2+ sessions | Repetition means a habit, not a one-off | | An approach that ended in a commit and a passing check | A proven solution | What demotes a rule: a newer correction that contradicts it (marked supersedes, no longer injected), or no use for a long time. How prompts are classified: cheap local rules first. Correction = pushback words at the start, or an interrupt. Acknowledgement = a short "ok / yes / do it" reply from a fixed list. Paste = fenced or JSON text, or very long. Question = ends in "?" or starts with how/what/why/can. Everything else = instruction. The small local model is used only for unclear cases, and only if the rules prove too noisy. "100% of the user's pattern" is not measurable as one number. What we measure instead: rule precision (of promoted rules, how many are right; target at least 90%, checked by hand on 50) and correction rate (with memory on, do you say "no, use X" less often?). The four categories and where each comes from: | Category | Holds | Source | When injected | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | User profile | Languages, formatter, test command, commit style, package manager | Repo config files and git log, not chat | Session start | | Project memory | Stack, DB, deploy target, decisions ("Neon, not local DB") | Corrections + repo files | Session start, this project only | | Session memory | Current goal, files touched, open todos, last error | Last session (exists: handover) | Session start | | Task history | Past tasks, how they ended, what you corrected | Labelled tasks (exists: recall) | Each prompt, top 3 by relevance | Record schema (v1): ```json { "id": "m_8f2c1a9e", "schema": 1, "kind": "project_fact", "scope": "project:/Users/aman/Developer/Paytmcall", "text": "Use Neon Postgres, not a local DB", "source": "correction", "evidence": ["ses_ab12:t4", "ses_cd34:t1"], "seen_in_sessions": 2, "confidence": 0.65, "first_seen": "2026-10-02", "last_seen": "2026-11-01", "supersedes": null } ``` - kind: profile \| project_fact \| decision \| correction \| task. - source: config \| git \| correction \| stated — how we know it. Config and git rank highest. - seen_in_sessions: how many separate sessions this fact appeared in. 2 or more (or read from config) = injected; 1 = a one-off, kept but not injected. - Same fact seen again: add evidence, raise confidence. A newer fact that contradicts an older one sets supersedes; the old one stops being injected but is kept. - Inject only facts seen at least twice, or read from config. Seen once means a one-off task, not a habit. Retrieval: filter by project, then BM25 (exists). Add embeddings and rank fusion only after a retrieval eval set shows BM25 missing relevant records. No vector database: SQLite with full-text search is enough at this size. Why the schema works across models: records become plain text in the prompt. Any model, local or cloud, reads text. Nothing in memory depends on the model. ### Memory pipeline: one assembly line, stage by stage Memory is one write pipeline plus two read paths, not many pipelines. Each stage is one plain function that takes the previous stage's output. Redaction always runs before anything reads the data; labelling runs once and feeds both memory and training data. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph W[Write: builds memory] A[Archive] --> R[Redact] --> S[Segment] --> C[Classify] --> L[Label tasks] --> X[Extract] --> M[Merge] --> SC[Score] --> ST[Store] end PR["Profile reader
repo config + git"] --> ST L --> TD[Training data] subgraph RD[Read: uses memory] F[Filter] --> B[BM25 search] --> P[Pick top 3] --> CB[Build context] --> I[Inject] end ST --> F I --> MOD[Active model] ``` Write stages: | # | Stage | Job | In → Out | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Archive | Keep a copy before Claude Code deletes it | session file → archived copy | To build | | 2 | Redact | Strip secrets | raw text → safe text | Built (memory); prototype (training) | | 3 | Segment | Split a session into tasks | session → tasks (prompt, files, commands, outcome) | Built | | 4 | Classify | Label each message | message → correction / instruction / question / paste / acknowledgement | Prototype (correction only) | | 5 | Label tasks | Mark each task accepted or rejected | task + next message → label | Prototype | | 6 | Extract | Pull candidate rules | corrections + config → candidate rules | To build | | 7 | Merge | Join duplicates, supersede old rules | candidates + existing rules → updated rules | To build | | 8 | Score | Rank rules | rules → scored rules | To build | | 9 | Store | Save to disk | → memory.json (tasks), rules.json (rules) | Tasks built; rules to build | | — | Profile reader | Read facts from the repo, not chat | lockfile, formatter config, scripts, git log → profile facts | To build | Read stages: | # | Stage | Job | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | R1 | Filter | Keep this project's items plus user-wide ones | Built (same-project boost) | | R2 | BM25 search | Rank past tasks by word match with the prompt | Built | | R3 | Pick | Top 3 above the threshold; skip ones already shown this session | Built | | R4 | Build context | Format rules, tasks and examples within the token budget | Partly built | | R5 | Inject | Add to session start or to the prompt | Built (Claude Code hooks, OpenCode plugin) | BM25 sits on the read side: it scores about 750 tasks in milliseconds when you type, so no pre-built search index is needed. Moving to BM25 + embeddings later changes stage R2 only. ### Worked example: one correction through the pipeline In Paytmcall you typed "why are we using local DB , use neon". 1. Archive and redact: the session is copied and secrets are removed first. 2. Segment: your previous ask plus Claude's work on it is task A; this message starts task B. 3. Classify: starts with "why are we using" → correction. Task A is labelled rejected and gets corrected: "why are we using local DB, use neon". 4. Extract: candidate rule in your own words, "use neon, not local DB"; scope project:/Users/aman/Developer/Paytmcall; source correction. No rewording, so nothing can be invented. 5. Merge: meaningful words (neon, local, db) are compared with existing rules in the same scope. Match → add evidence, seen_in_sessions goes up. Same subject, opposite choice → newer wins, old one is superseded. No match → new candidate with seen_in_sessions: 1. 6. Score: see the formula below. 7. Store, then use: next time anyone asks "set up the database" in Paytmcall, the rule is in context at session start, and recall shows task A with "user then corrected: use neon". ### Scoring ```javascript score = source weight × repetition × recency source: config 1.0 · git 0.9 · correction 0.8 · stated 0.5 repetition: min(1, seen_in_sessions / 3) recency: halves every ~60 days without being seen again ``` A correction seen in 2 sessions scores about 0.53 and is injected. Seen once, it scores about 0.27: stored, not injected. ### Profile facts from the repo (no talk needed) Read fresh at every session start, so they never go stale. Source weight 1.0, the most trusted facts. | Fact | Read from | | --- | --- | | Package manager | Lockfile (pnpm-lock.yaml → pnpm) | | Test, lint, build commands | package.json scripts, pyproject.toml | | Formatting | .prettierrc, ruff or black config | | Strictness | tsconfig.json strict | | Commit style | Last 50 commit messages | ### Storage ```javascript ~/.footprint/archive/ raw sessions, redacted (never injected) ~/.footprint/memory.json task history index (exists today) ~/.footprint/rules.json promoted rules, schema v1 (to build) /AGENTS.md generated block of this project's rules, between markers (opt-in, later) ``` ### Token budgets | When | What | Budget | | --- | --- | --- | | Session start | Rules + profile, highest score first, this project plus user-wide | \~400 tokens | | Session start | Handover (last session's state) | \~800 tokens | | Every prompt | Top 3 similar past tasks with "user then corrected" + 1–2 of your own diffs (\~40 lines each) | \~800 tokens | ### Guards against bad memory | Risk | Guard | | --- | --- | | Wrong rule repeated every session | Inject only with evidence; footprint memory list / forget to remove it | | Old decision, project moved on | Newer contradiction supersedes it; recency decay | | One project's rule leaks into another | Scope: project rules show only in their project; user-wide needs 2+ projects | | Context bloat | Fixed token budgets; ranked cut-off | | Secrets | Redacted before anything is indexed | | Bench answers leaking into memory | Held-out bench sessions excluded (built) | | Paraphrases not merged ("use neon" vs "switch to serverless postgres") | Accept for now; add embeddings only if the precision check shows duplicates | ### Memory build plan Nothing technical blocks this. Memory does not depend on the hardware, model or LoRA decisions. Settle before building: | Item | Why it matters | Default | | --- | --- | --- | | Build on the prototype branch | Labeller and training redaction already exist on worktree-distill-pipeline; main lacks them | Yes: continue there, then merge | | Write AGENTS.md into repos | Changes files inside your projects | Off at first; hooks only; opt-in later | | Stop Claude Code deleting old sessions | Edits ~/.claude/settings.json (cleanupPeriodDays) | Yes, with your approval of the edit | | Small bench (1 task) | Blocks proving memory helps (B beats A), not building it | Grow the bench alongside | Build order, each step tested before the next: 1. Archive: copy all existing and new sessions, redacted. 2. Classifier and labels: merge the prototype; add question, paste and acknowledgement types. 3. Profile reader: lockfile, formatter, test command, commit style. 4. Rules store: extract from corrections, merge, supersede, score → rules.json. 5. Injection: rules and profile at session start, within the token budget. 6. footprint memory list / forget: remove a wrong rule by hand. 7. Check: rule precision on your data (you mark each listed rule right or wrong) and a correction-rate baseline. Real runs use your data in a temp folder, so live memory is untouched until merge.

7. LoRA design

The LoRA should learn how you work — code shape, naming, the order you read, edit and test — from evidence you accepted. It should not learn facts; memory carries those. What goes into training: | Example type | Input | Target | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Accepted turn | Prompt + context | Assistant turn you didn't push back on | Prototype built | | Committed diff | Task prompt + file before | Diff that reached a commit | To build | | Your own code | Commit message + file before | Your hand-written change | To build, best style signal | | Rejected turn | — | Excluded now; saved as pairs for preference training later | Prototype excludes it | Training setup (starting point, change only on measured gain): - Base model: the active model from the registry (section 8), not hard-coded. - Format: the model's native chat template and native tool-call format. Today's custom format is never used by OpenCode at runtime, so the adapter learns a protocol nobody speaks. - Loss on the assistant's tokens only (--mask-prompt in mlx-lm). - Rank 8–16, alpha 2× rank, attention and MLP layers, 1–2 passes, stop early on validation loss. - Run in the background at low priority, only on new data, at most weekly. Training heats the laptop. Versioning and approval: ```javascript adapters//v3/adapters.safetensors adapters//v3/metrics.json # data hash, loss, bench scores adapters//active -> v2 # switch only after the gate passes ``` Rollback means pointing active back to an earlier version. A new version becomes active only if it passes the gate in section 9. Honest expectation: on a 1.5B–3B model, a LoRA will not match a cloud model at finishing tasks. Its realistic value is style and convention. If the bench shows no gain over memory alone, keep LoRA optional. ### 8. Personalisation framework: how it works Five layers, cheapest and most reliable first. Layers 1–4 work with every model; layer 5 is optional and local only. | # | Layer | What it carries | When it runs | Needs training? | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Rules file (AGENTS.md section generated from memory) | Standing rules: "use Neon, not a local DB", package manager, test command | Read by the model at session start | No | | 2 | Session handover + memory rules | Last session's state; promoted rules for this project | Session start | No | | 3 | Recall + your own examples | Top 3 similar past tasks, plus 1–2 of your accepted diffs for similar files | Every prompt | No | | 4 | Formatter / linter hook | Your repo's own formatting and lint config | After every edit the model makes | No | | 5 | LoRA adapter (optional) | Hard-to-describe habits: code shape, naming, change size | Every request to the local model | Yes, weekly at most, behind the gate | ```mermaid flowchart TD S[Session starts] --> L1["1. Rules file + 2. handover and memory rules"] L1 --> P[You type a prompt] P --> L3["3. Recall: similar past tasks + your own diffs"] L3 --> M["Active model (local or cloud)
5. + LoRA adapter if local and approved"] M --> E[Model edits files] E --> L4["4. Formatter / linter fixes style"] L4 --> N[Your next prompt] N --> LB["Labeller: accepted / rejected"] LB --> MEM[Memory updated] LB --> TD[Training data updated] MEM --> L1 TD -.-> W["Weekly, optional: train LoRA → bench gate → activate"] W -.-> M N --> L3 ``` The loop closes itself: every reply you give labels the previous answer, which updates memory immediately and training data for the next optional LoRA run. ### Requirements to run it locally Hardware: | Setup | Minimum | What it allows | | --- | --- | --- | | Layers 1–4 with a cloud model | Any machine that runs OpenCode or Claude Code | Full framework except the local model | | Layers 1–5 with a 1.5B local model | 8 GB Apple Silicon (your M1) | Run and train LoRA on 1.5B, 4-bit | | 3–4B local model + LoRA | 16 GB recommended | Better local model; training is tight on 8 GB | | 9B local model + LoRA | 32 GB | Realistic upgrade path | Software (all local, all existing tools): - Python 3.10+ (you have 3.13). Memory, labeller and recall use the standard library only. - Git: for commit and revert signals and your own diffs. - OpenCode and/or Claude Code, plus footprint's plugin and hooks (already built). - Your repo's own formatter and linter (prettier, eslint, ruff…). Run through OpenCode's formatter setting or a Claude Code post-edit hook (exact setup to verify). - mlx-lm: only for layer 5 (local model and LoRA). Storage (measured 2026-11-04): - Transcripts: 93 MB across 30 sessions. The archive roughly doubles this; small. - Memory index: under 1 MB. - Base model 1.5B, 4-bit: about 1 GB. Each adapter version: about 21 MB. Data needed before each layer is useful: | Layer | Minimum data | | --- | --- | | 1–2 Rules and handover | 1 session; rules need a fact seen in 2+ sessions or in config | | 3 Your own examples | About 20 committed tasks in the project | | 4 Formatter hook | The repo's existing config; no history needed | | 5 LoRA | At least 3 sessions and about 500 accepted examples; 30+ bench tasks before the gate can judge it | Privacy: everything stays under ~/.footprint and the repo. No data leaves the machine; vault sync of training data is off unless you opt in. ## 9. Intelligence layer Pick the model last, behind a small registry, so memory and the pipeline never depend on it. The hardware decides which models are even possible. Model registry (one small file, no framework): ```json {"active": "qwen2.5-coder-1.5b", "models": { "qwen2.5-coder-1.5b": {"mlx": "mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct-4bit", "min_ram_gb": 8, "trainable": true} }} ``` footprint model use switches the active model, and its adapter if one exists for that model. Memory is unchanged. Cloud models (Big Pickle, GLM, Gemini) get memory but no adapter. What fits in memory (approximate: weights only, about 2 bytes per parameter at bf16 and about 0.55 at 4-bit): | Model size | bf16 weights | 4-bit weights | 8 GB M1: run | 8 GB M1: train LoRA | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1.5B | \~3 GB | \~0.9 GB | Yes | Yes | | 3–4B | \~7 GB | \~2 GB | 4-bit only | 4-bit, tight | | 9B | \~18 GB | \~5 GB | 4-bit, very tight | No | | 26–31B | \~55–62 GB | \~15–17 GB | No | No | Only about 5–6 GB of the 8 GB is usable after macOS. So on this machine, quantisation is not optional above about 2B. "Higher precision first" needs 32 GB or more. Candidates from the proposal (names, sizes and licences still to verify before use): - Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B — current baseline, fits today. - Qwen3.5 9B and 27B — 9B is the realistic upgrade on a 16–32 GB machine. - Gemma 4 — check whether a 12B exists; the 26B A4B mixture-of-experts still needs all weights in memory. - NVIDIA Nemotron — check which coding checkpoint and its licence. Decide with the bench, not with leaderboards: same tasks, same memory, each model. ## 10. Evaluation Nothing is called an improvement until the bench shows it. The bench already exists; it needs more tasks and personalisation metrics. Experiments (same tasks, same repo state, same tools): | Run | Memory | LoRA | Answers | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A | off | off | Baseline | | B | on | off | What memory adds | | C | off | on | What LoRA adds | | D | on | on | Combined | Metrics: | Group | Metric | How measured | | --- | --- | --- | | Coding | Task pass rate | Bench: the original check passes and at least one file changed | | Personalisation | Style match | Lint and format errors of the model's diff against the repo's own config | | Personalisation | Closeness to your accepted change | Edit distance to the diff you actually committed | | Personalisation | Correction rate in real use | Corrective follow-up prompts per task, read from logs (labeller from section 5) | | Memory | Retrieval hit rate | Was the relevant past task in the top 3? Needs a small labelled set | | System | Latency, peak RAM, training time | Logged per run | Approval gate for a new adapter: - [ ] Validation loss lower than the active adapter on the session-split test set - [ ] Bench pass rate not lower than the active adapter - [ ] Style match not worse - [ ] At least 30 bench tasks, so the numbers mean something Data rules: the newest sessions are the test set and are never trained on. Bench tasks are held out from memory and training (already true). ## 11. Roadmap Five phases in strict order; each starts only when the previous gate passes. Phase 1 is small and removes the privacy risk, so it comes first. ```mermaid flowchart TD P1["1. Data hygiene (start here)
Redact training data; split by session
Keep data local; archive transcripts"] --> G1{{"Gate: 0 secret hits; archive captures every new session"}} G1 --> P2["2. Labeller and bench
Accept/reject labels from chat and git
Grow the bench to 30+ tasks; style and correction metrics"] P2 --> G2{{"Gate: labels spot-checked on 50 tasks; bench has 30+ tasks"}} G2 --> P3["3. Memory facts
Profile from repo config and git; facts from corrections
Merge, supersede, inject under a budget"] P3 --> G3{{"Gate: experiment B (memory) beats A"}} G3 --> P4["4. LoRA v2
Native chat and tool format; accepted turns + your commits
Versioned adapters, rollback, background training"] P4 --> G4{{"Gate: C or D beats B; adapter passes approval checks"}} G4 --> P5["5. Model choice
Registry and switching; hardware decision first
Compare on the same bench and memory"] P5 --> G5{{"Gate: the bench picks the default model"}} style P1 fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#2b6cb0,stroke-width:2px ``` Phase 2 is the hardest: git-based labels (commits, reverts, your own code) are the most reliable signal and the most work. If phase 3 gives most of the gain, phase 4 can wait. These decide scope; building before answering them risks rework. Torch/PEFT on Linux and Windows (rank 8, alpha 16). | backends/ | | Local server | OpenAI-compatible API on port 8399, auto-started by launchd/systemd. | service.py | | Bench | Replays your own finished tasks (ended in a commit and a passing check) with any model, memory on or off. Held-out sessions stay out of memory and training. | bench.py | | Vault | API keys plus sync of data/ and adapters/ to a private GitHub repo. | vault.py | | Website | Sign-in, API keys, setup steps, bench reports and share badges. | UI-Web/ | State of the data on this machine (measured 2026-11-03): - data/train.jsonl: 3942 examples; 484 match a secret pattern. - Adapter: trained on Jul 15 for 100 iterations, about 2.5% of one pass over the data. It has learned almost nothing. - Bench: 1 qualifying task, so no reliable score yet. - Claude transcripts on disk: 30 sessions across 18 projects. ## 3. Gaps: today vs target The biggest gaps are in what the LoRA learns and in privacy; memory and evaluation are partly there. | Pillar | Exists today | Missing | Severity | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Privacy | Redaction in memory | Redaction in training data; sync uploads raw training data to GitHub | Critical | | Personalisation (LoRA) | Collect, train, serve | Trains on Claude's turns, including rejected ones. No accept/reject labels, no use of your own commits, custom tool format the client never uses, no versioning or rollback | High | | Personalisation (data) | Reads live transcripts | Own archive of all existing and new transcripts; raise cleanupPeriodDays. Claude Code deletes transcripts after about 30 days by default, which is why training data fell from 3942 to about 1100 examples. Already-deleted sessions survive only as fragments in the old data/train.jsonl: redact and keep it | High | | Memory | Session memory (handover), task memory (BM25 recall) | User profile, project facts, corrections, scoring, merging, schema version | Medium | | Retrieval | BM25, same-project boost, fixed threshold | Embeddings, rank fusion, retrieval eval set | Low (until measured) | | Intelligence | One hard-coded model per platform | Model registry, switching, hardware check, per-model adapters | Medium | | Evaluation | Bench with memory on/off | Enough tasks (30+), personalisation metrics, LoRA arms, approval gate | High | | Isolation | One OS user = one ~/.footprint | Fine for local use; nothing more needed now | None | ## 4. Target architecture Every session passes one labeller; its labels decide what becomes training data and what becomes memory. The model sits at the end and can be swapped. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Claude Code sessions] --> D C[Git history, repo config] --> D D["Archive and redact
local copy kept; secrets removed first"] --> E E["Pattern labeller
each task: accepted, rejected or user-authored"] --> F E --> G F["Curated training data
accepted work only, split by session"] --> H G["Structured memory
profile, project, session, task history"] --> I H["LoRA adapter
per user, per model; versioned"] -- "if it passes the bench gate" --> J I["Context builder
BM25 top matches, ~1500-token budget"] -- "selected context only" --> J J["Active model
local Qwen with its adapter, or any cloud model"] style E fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#2b6cb0,stroke-width:2px ``` Memory reaches every model as text. The adapter reaches only the local model it was trained for, and only after it passes the bench gate. Cloud models get memory only. ## 5. The pipeline, stage by stage One pipeline reads each session once and produces two separate outputs: curated training data and structured memory. The pattern labeller in the middle is the core of the whole system. | # | Stage | Input | Output | Rule | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Archive | Claude Code .jsonl, OpenCode DB | Local copy in ~/.footprint/archive/ | First run: copy every existing session still on disk (30 today). After that: copy each new session as it ends. Also set cleanupPeriodDays high in ~/.claude/settings.json so Claude Code stops deleting them. | | 2 | Redact | Archived session | Same session, secrets replaced | Runs before anything else reads the data. Nothing unredacted leaves this stage. | | 3 | Segment | Session | Tasks: one real prompt plus everything until the next | Already exists in memory.py. | | 4 | Label (pattern recognition) | Task + the user's next prompt + git history | accepted, rejected, user-authored, or unknown | See the signal table below. | | 5a | Curate for training | Accepted and user-authored tasks | train / valid / test split by session, newest = test | Cap examples per session; remove near-duplicates. | | 5b | Extract for memory | All labelled tasks + repo config | Memory records (section 6) | Merge repeats, track evidence and confidence. | | 6 | Use | Memory records, adapter | Context for the active model | Model-independent text; adapter only for its own model. | Signals the labeller uses: | Signal | Label | Measured on your history | | --- | --- | --- | | Your next prompt pushes back ("no…", "still broken", "why are we using X") | rejected | 59 of about 1160 turns | | You interrupted the answer | rejected | included above | | You moved on to a new ask | accepted (weak) | most turns | | AI edit survives into a commit | accepted (strong) | not built yet | | git checkout / git restore right after an AI edit | rejected (strong) | not built yet | | Code you committed that no AI edit produced | user-authored (best style signal) | not built yet | The last three need git, not chat. They are the most reliable signals, and the hardest part to build. ## 6. Memory design One record format for all four categories, stored as local JSON. Retrieval decides what reaches the prompt, under a fixed budget of about 1500 tokens. Important vs vague: the rule. A sentence becomes a memory rule only when there is evidence you acted on it. We never judge by how important it sounds. How your 747 past prompts split (measured 2026-11-04):
Type Message count Example What memory does with it
Instruction 457 (61%) "add a call recording button" Task history only; a one-off, not a rule
Question 196 (26%) "how is memory working?" Dropped as a fact; the answer is Claude's words, not your preference
Paste 49 (7%) logs, JSON, specs Dropped; not your voice
Acknowledgement 22 (3%) "ok do it", "cool" Dropped as content; used as a label that the previous answer was accepted
Correction 23 (3%) "why are we using local DB, use neon" Kept as a rule; strongest signal
About 97% of the talk never becomes a rule. Three tiers: 1. Raw archive: everything, redacted. Never injected; only used to rebuild the tiers below. 2. Task history: one small record per task (ask, files, outcome, what you corrected). Retrieved only when a new prompt is similar, top 3. 3. Rules: promoted only with evidence, injected at every session start under the budget. What promotes a sentence to a rule (strongest first): | Evidence | Why it counts | | --- | --- | | Repo config or git (lockfile, formatter config, test script, commit style) | It is what you actually do; no talk needed | | A correction | You rejected something and named what you want | | The same instruction in 2+ sessions | Repetition means a habit, not a one-off | | An approach that ended in a commit and a passing check | A proven solution | What demotes a rule: a newer correction that contradicts it (marked supersedes, no longer injected), or no use for a long time. How prompts are classified: cheap local rules first. Correction = pushback words at the start, or an interrupt. Acknowledgement = a short "ok / yes / do it" reply from a fixed list. Paste = fenced or JSON text, or very long. Question = ends in "?" or starts with how/what/why/can. Everything else = instruction. The small local model is used only for unclear cases, and only if the rules prove too noisy. "100% of the user's pattern" is not measurable as one number. What we measure instead: rule precision (of promoted rules, how many are right; target at least 90%, checked by hand on 50) and correction rate (with memory on, do you say "no, use X" less often?). The four categories and where each comes from: | Category | Holds | Source | When injected | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | User profile | Languages, formatter, test command, commit style, package manager | Repo config files and git log, not chat | Session start | | Project memory | Stack, DB, deploy target, decisions ("Neon, not local DB") | Corrections + repo files | Session start, this project only | | Session memory | Current goal, files touched, open todos, last error | Last session (exists: handover) | Session start | | Task history | Past tasks, how they ended, what you corrected | Labelled tasks (exists: recall) | Each prompt, top 3 by relevance | Record schema (v1): ```json { "id": "m_8f2c1a9e", "schema": 1, "kind": "project_fact", "scope": "project:/Users/aman/Developer/Paytmcall", "text": "Use Neon Postgres, not a local DB", "source": "correction", "evidence": ["ses_ab12:t4", "ses_cd34:t1"], "seen_in_sessions": 2, "confidence": 0.65, "first_seen": "2026-10-02", "last_seen": "2026-11-01", "supersedes": null } ``` - kind: profile \| project_fact \| decision \| correction \| task. - source: config \| git \| correction \| stated — how we know it. Config and git rank highest. - seen_in_sessions: how many separate sessions this fact appeared in. 2 or more (or read from config) = injected; 1 = a one-off, kept but not injected. - Same fact seen again: add evidence, raise confidence. A newer fact that contradicts an older one sets supersedes; the old one stops being injected but is kept. - Inject only facts seen at least twice, or read from config. Seen once means a one-off task, not a habit. Retrieval: filter by project, then BM25 (exists). Add embeddings and rank fusion only after a retrieval eval set shows BM25 missing relevant records. No vector database: SQLite with full-text search is enough at this size. Why the schema works across models: records become plain text in the prompt. Any model, local or cloud, reads text. Nothing in memory depends on the model. ### Memory pipeline: one assembly line, stage by stage Memory is one write pipeline plus two read paths, not many pipelines. Each stage is one plain function that takes the previous stage's output. Redaction always runs before anything reads the data; labelling runs once and feeds both memory and training data. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph W[Write: builds memory] A[Archive] --> R[Redact] --> S[Segment] --> C[Classify] --> L[Label tasks] --> X[Extract] --> M[Merge] --> SC[Score] --> ST[Store] end PR["Profile reader
repo config + git"] --> ST L --> TD[Training data] subgraph RD[Read: uses memory] F[Filter] --> B[BM25 search] --> P[Pick top 3] --> CB[Build context] --> I[Inject] end ST --> F I --> MOD[Active model] ``` Write stages: | # | Stage | Job | In → Out | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Archive | Keep a copy before Claude Code deletes it | session file → archived copy | To build | | 2 | Redact | Strip secrets | raw text → safe text | Built (memory); prototype (training) | | 3 | Segment | Split a session into tasks | session → tasks (prompt, files, commands, outcome) | Built | | 4 | Classify | Label each message | message → correction / instruction / question / paste / acknowledgement | Prototype (correction only) | | 5 | Label tasks | Mark each task accepted or rejected | task + next message → label | Prototype | | 6 | Extract | Pull candidate rules | corrections + config → candidate rules | To build | | 7 | Merge | Join duplicates, supersede old rules | candidates + existing rules → updated rules | To build | | 8 | Score | Rank rules | rules → scored rules | To build | | 9 | Store | Save to disk | → memory.json (tasks), rules.json (rules) | Tasks built; rules to build | | — | Profile reader | Read facts from the repo, not chat | lockfile, formatter config, scripts, git log → profile facts | To build | Read stages: | # | Stage | Job | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | R1 | Filter | Keep this project's items plus user-wide ones | Built (same-project boost) | | R2 | BM25 search | Rank past tasks by word match with the prompt | Built | | R3 | Pick | Top 3 above the threshold; skip ones already shown this session | Built | | R4 | Build context | Format rules, tasks and examples within the token budget | Partly built | | R5 | Inject | Add to session start or to the prompt | Built (Claude Code hooks, OpenCode plugin) | BM25 sits on the read side: it scores about 750 tasks in milliseconds when you type, so no pre-built search index is needed. Moving to BM25 + embeddings later changes stage R2 only. ### Worked example: one correction through the pipeline In Paytmcall you typed "why are we using local DB , use neon". 1. Archive and redact: the session is copied and secrets are removed first. 2. Segment: your previous ask plus Claude's work on it is task A; this message starts task B. 3. Classify: starts with "why are we using" → correction. Task A is labelled rejected and gets corrected: "why are we using local DB, use neon". 4. Extract: candidate rule in your own words, "use neon, not local DB"; scope project:/Users/aman/Developer/Paytmcall; source correction. No rewording, so nothing can be invented. 5. Merge: meaningful words (neon, local, db) are compared with existing rules in the same scope. Match → add evidence, seen_in_sessions goes up. Same subject, opposite choice → newer wins, old one is superseded. No match → new candidate with seen_in_sessions: 1. 6. Score: see the formula below. 7. Store, then use: next time anyone asks "set up the database" in Paytmcall, the rule is in context at session start, and recall shows task A with "user then corrected: use neon". ### Scoring ```javascript score = source weight × repetition × recency source: config 1.0 · git 0.9 · correction 0.8 · stated 0.5 repetition: min(1, seen_in_sessions / 3) recency: halves every ~60 days without being seen again ``` A correction seen in 2 sessions scores about 0.53 and is injected. Seen once, it scores about 0.27: stored, not injected. ### Profile facts from the repo (no talk needed) Read fresh at every session start, so they never go stale. Source weight 1.0, the most trusted facts. | Fact | Read from | | --- | --- | | Package manager | Lockfile (pnpm-lock.yaml → pnpm) | | Test, lint, build commands | package.json scripts, pyproject.toml | | Formatting | .prettierrc, ruff or black config | | Strictness | tsconfig.json strict | | Commit style | Last 50 commit messages | ### Storage ```javascript ~/.footprint/archive/ raw sessions, redacted (never injected) ~/.footprint/memory.json task history index (exists today) ~/.footprint/rules.json promoted rules, schema v1 (to build) /AGENTS.md generated block of this project's rules, between markers (opt-in, later) ``` ### Token budgets | When | What | Budget | | --- | --- | --- | | Session start | Rules + profile, highest score first, this project plus user-wide | \~400 tokens | | Session start | Handover (last session's state) | \~800 tokens | | Every prompt | Top 3 similar past tasks with "user then corrected" + 1–2 of your own diffs (\~40 lines each) | \~800 tokens | ### Guards against bad memory | Risk | Guard | | --- | --- | | Wrong rule repeated every session | Inject only with evidence; footprint memory list / forget to remove it | | Old decision, project moved on | Newer contradiction supersedes it; recency decay | | One project's rule leaks into another | Scope: project rules show only in their project; user-wide needs 2+ projects | | Context bloat | Fixed token budgets; ranked cut-off | | Secrets | Redacted before anything is indexed | | Bench answers leaking into memory | Held-out bench sessions excluded (built) | | Paraphrases not merged ("use neon" vs "switch to serverless postgres") | Accept for now; add embeddings only if the precision check shows duplicates | ### Memory build plan Nothing technical blocks this. Memory does not depend on the hardware, model or LoRA decisions. Settle before building: | Item | Why it matters | Default | | --- | --- | --- | | Build on the prototype branch | Labeller and training redaction already exist on worktree-distill-pipeline; main lacks them | Yes: continue there, then merge | | Write AGENTS.md into repos | Changes files inside your projects | Off at first; hooks only; opt-in later | | Stop Claude Code deleting old sessions | Edits ~/.claude/settings.json (cleanupPeriodDays) | Yes, with your approval of the edit | | Small bench (1 task) | Blocks proving memory helps (B beats A), not building it | Grow the bench alongside | Build order, each step tested before the next: 1. Archive: copy all existing and new sessions, redacted. 2. Classifier and labels: merge the prototype; add question, paste and acknowledgement types. 3. Profile reader: lockfile, formatter, test command, commit style. 4. Rules store: extract from corrections, merge, supersede, score → rules.json. 5. Injection: rules and profile at session start, within the token budget. 6. footprint memory list / forget: remove a wrong rule by hand. 7. Check: rule precision on your data (you mark each listed rule right or wrong) and a correction-rate baseline. Real runs use your data in a temp folder, so live memory is untouched until merge.

7. LoRA design

The LoRA should learn how you work — code shape, naming, the order you read, edit and test — from evidence you accepted. It should not learn facts; memory carries those. What goes into training: | Example type | Input | Target | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Accepted turn | Prompt + context | Assistant turn you didn't push back on | Prototype built | | Committed diff | Task prompt + file before | Diff that reached a commit | To build | | Your own code | Commit message + file before | Your hand-written change | To build, best style signal | | Rejected turn | — | Excluded now; saved as pairs for preference training later | Prototype excludes it | Training setup (starting point, change only on measured gain): - Base model: the active model from the registry (section 8), not hard-coded. - Format: the model's native chat template and native tool-call format. Training heats the laptop. Versioning and approval: ```javascript adapters//v3/adapters.safetensors adapters//v3/metrics.json # data hash, loss, bench scores adapters//active -> v2 # switch only after the gate passes ``` Rollback means pointing active back to an earlier version. A new version becomes active only if it passes the gate in section 9. Honest expectation: on a 1.5B–3B model, a LoRA will not match a cloud model at finishing tasks. 5. + LoRA adapter if local and approved"] M --> E[Model edits files] E --> L4["4. Formatter / linter fixes style"] L4 --> N[Your next prompt] N --> LB["Labeller: accepted / rejected"] LB --> MEM[Memory updated] LB --> TD[Training data updated] MEM --> L1 TD -.-> W["Weekly, optional: train LoRA → bench gate → activate"] W -.-> M N --> L3 ``` The loop closes itself: every reply you give labels the previous answer, which updates memory immediately and training data for the next optional LoRA run. ### Requirements to run it locally Hardware: | Setup | Minimum | What it allows | | --- | --- | --- | | Layers 1–4 with a cloud model | Any machine that runs OpenCode or Claude Code | Full framework except the local model | | Layers 1–5 with a 1.5B local model | 8 GB Apple Silicon (your M1) | Run and train LoRA on 1.5B, 4-bit | | 3–4B local model + LoRA | 16 GB recommended | Better local model; training is tight on 8 GB | | 9B local model + LoRA | 32 GB | Realistic upgrade path | Software (all local, all existing tools): - Python 3.10+ (you have 3.13).
